1.answer: When adding: compute k positions and set all those bits to 1. When checking: compute k positions and look at the bits. If any is 0, definitely not added; if all are 1, probably added.
1.quote: Add an item: compute its k positions and set all of those bits to 1. Check an item: compute its k positions and look at the bits.

2.answer: Can give false positives (saying yes when no), never false negatives (saying no when yes), because bits are set to 1 and never go back to 0.
2.quote: So the error only goes one way. 'No' is always trustworthy, and 'yes' means 'check properly if it matters'.

3.answer: Clearing bits might erase bits that other items depend on, causing those items to be wrongly rejected (false negatives).
3.quote: Setting an item's bits back to 0 might erase bits that other items also depend on, and then those items would get false negatives.

4.answer: It answers 'probably added' (yes), which is wrong—a false positive—since all k positions will be 1 regardless of whether the item was actually added.
4.quote: If all of them are 1, the item was probably added.

excess: A billion URLs of about 60 bytes each comes to roughly 60 GB before any overhead.
A database keeps a Bloom filter for each file on disk. Before reading a file to look for a key, it asks the filter.
A web cache only stores a page the second time it's requested. A Bloom filter of 'URLs seen once' answers 'have I seen this before?' cheaply.
A variant called a counting Bloom filter stores a small counter in each slot instead of a single bit.
